newsitem.title: USA: Korea peace talks briefing could be delayed again.
newsitem.headline: Korea peace talks briefing could be delayed again.

text.p: North Korea could further delay a briefing in New York on proposed Korean peninsula peace talks because of inconclusive talks over a grain deal for Pyongyang, U.S. officials said Friday.

North Korea this week delayed the briefing, in which details for the peace talks were to be thrashed out. The peace talks, grouping the United States, China and the two Koreas, were proposed by Washington and Seoul last April.
The briefing was originally set for Wednesday but Pyongyang, seeking a barter deal for 500,000 metric tons of grain with U.S. grain trader Cargill Inc, asked that the meeting be delayed until Feb 5.

"Latest reports are that unless North Korea receives more grain or gets grain for the Cargill deal...they have no intention of going to the briefing," U.S. ambassador to South Korea James Laney told a news conference in Seoul.
"That puts a great deal of doubt on the four-party talks."
State Department officials in Washington appeared less pessimistic, but admitted it was now unclear whether the briefing could go ahead next week.

"The reason is the North Korean diplomats haven't shown up in Beijing yet to get their visas from the United States embassy," one official said. "That's exactly what happened last week." The United States has no embassy in Pyongyang.

North Korea, following months of resistance, agreed in December to attend the crucial U.S.-South Korean briefing after negotiations with Washington that led to a Pyongyang apology for a September submarine incursion into the South.
The negotiations paved the way for Cargill to receive a permit from Washington to barter grain for North Korean minerals.
The shipment is crucial for Pyongyang, which is suffering an acute food shortage after severe floods in 1995 and 1996.

But Laney said no deal had yet been struck between Cargill and Pyongyang. "As yet, Cargill has not found a sufficient basis for that barter. The United States government of course has nothing to do with private business," he said.
In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States had no immediate plans to make a direct food shipment to North Korea.
Burns also denied press reports that the United States and North Korea had agreed to set up liaison offices in each other's capitals by July.
"We've not agreed to any specific date for it. There are still some logistical issues that need to be worked out," Burns told a news briefing.

The two countries agreed in principle in Oct. 1994 to set up liaison offices. The United States has sent a diplomat, Evans Revere, to South Korea to learn Korean so that he can take over the U.S. office in Pyongyang when it opens.
